newsitem.title: USA: Economy lifts gasoline but U.S. demand seen easing.
newsitem.headline: Economy lifts gasoline but U.S. demand seen easing.

text.p: The recent surge in gasoline demand is largely being driven by a strong U.S. economy, which has given more and more Americans the confidence to take off for vacation in their cars, said economists.
But the high demand rate for motor fuel is expected to slide in late August when children begin to return to school.

"This is one of the strongest 'driving seasons' we've ever seen," said an economist for the Department of Energy, who did not wish to be named. "We are running several hundred thousand barrels per day over last year."
The American Automobile Association says gasoline sales are running about two percent above last year but the spurt may be short, ending late August.
Traditionally demand picks up around Memorial Day in late May and begins to tail off soon after the July 4 weekend.

"People feel free to take longer trips or more trips this year. The economy is good," William Berman, a spokesman for the national auto group, said. "But it is a short-term growth and should slide in August," Berman added.

Gross domestic product, the broadest measure of overall U.S. economic activity, slowed abruptly in the second quarter with growth put at 2.2 percent, the Commerce Department said on Thursday. But it followed a first quarter gain of 4.9 percent.
The GDP, combined with a booming stock market, low inflation and a low unemployment rate has given many people the confidence that they can afford to hit the road.

According to the DoE, gasoline demand for the past six months has been running at a relatively steady rate of between 40,000 to 50,000 barrels per day (bpd) above the equivalent 1996 levels. But in July there was a sudden jump to 300,000 barrels, which has refused to let up.
"I've been observing these stats for a long time and (this jump) is unprecedented," said Nizam Sharief, director of energy research at Hornsby & Co.

According to the American Petroleum Institute, an industry group based in Washington D.C., demand in the first quarter was actually below the previous year's level but then was running 2.8 percent over year-ago for the second quarter. In the four weeks leading to July 25, implied demand jumped to 5.9 percent over year-ago levels.
"I'm kind of flabbergasted. I have no explanation why except maybe everyone decided to take vacation at the same time," said Sharief, echoing comments by other economists.

Sharief said he expects implied demand -- which has been as high as 8.8 million bpd -- to level off at the 8.4 to 8.6 million bpd level for the next couple of weeks and then fall off at the end of August.
"There will be a dramatic turnaround in gasoline demand," said Sharief. "Demand will fall off quickly and then we will see a tremendous inventory build number."
